5. Management fee, carried interest, hurdle and GP commitment.
6. Portfolio construction: target number of companies, average and maximum cheque size, reserve policy, and current boards per investment partner.
7. Beyond yourself, who drives sourcing, underwriting and value creation, and whom the key person clause names.

Happy to take these on a call if that is quicker.

criteria.title: A single, compressed close window
criteria.preference: Underwrite a new Private Growth fund through the defined framework - edge, downside-first stress, team and succession, portfolio construction, terms and monitoring triggers - before committing.
criteria.rationale: An evidenced underwrite takes a defined amount of work, and the house rule (GP-03) is to test a manager's live answers against prior materials rather than accept the marketing framing; a closing timetable that does not allow the framework to be completed forces the decision onto the manager's narrative instead of onto evidence.
criteria.finding: First close is approaching the end of 2026 and 'may serve as final close due to strong demand'; the only diligence channel offered is virtual data room (VDR) access, and the demand claim is the manager's own, with no independent corroboration in the materials.
criteria.source: Intro email / key facts
criteria.assessment: A fit only if the manager confirms that a subsequent closing will be available after the end-of-2026 first close, because on the materials as they stand the whole underwrite (edge, downside, team, terms, portfolio construction) would have to be completed inside one window on the strength of a demand claim only the manager has made.

criteria.title: First-close discount, quantified
criteria.preference: Quantify the fee saving available from a first close or size break, and treat terms as both a net-return lever and an alignment tool.
criteria.rationale: Fee terms are a permanent drag on net return, and the first close is the one point in a fundraise at which an investor has leverage to change them; the practice is to state the saving as a number rather than to accept 'standard terms'.
criteria.finding: The materials state no management fee, carried interest, hurdle, general partner (GP) commitment or first-close discount, while the fund sits at the exact moment the preference has leverage.
criteria.source: Intro email / key facts (no economics disclosed)
criteria.assessment: A fit only if a quantified first-close or relationship discount is agreed before the end-of-2026 close, since the materials disclose no fee, carry, hurdle or GP commitment at all and the closing date is the point at which that leverage disappears.

criteria.title: Repeatable, structural edge
criteria.preference: The answer to 'why them?' must be a concrete, repeatable structural advantage in sourcing, information, operations or execution at scale.
criteria.rationale: Where the edge is not structural and repeatable, the fund is underwritten as commodity beta and should be priced as commodity beta or passed; a geography and a fund number are not, by themselves, an edge.
criteria.finding: The materials describe the fund only by geography (Japan), fund number (10) and a 'macro/policy coordination component'; no sourcing mechanism, proprietary data asset, network or in-house operating capability is described.
criteria.source: Intro email / key facts
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the materials name no sourcing, information or operating mechanism at all; what would settle it is the proportion of deals sourced bilaterally or pre-emptively, pipeline-to-completion conversion rates, and the named in-house resource that delivers value after investment.

criteria.title: What the 'macro/policy coordination component' actually is
criteria.preference: Avoid 'go anywhere' mandates without guardrails, and classify the strategy before underwriting it: Private Growth requires an equity-like engine, while Diversifiers requires returns explained by non-equity, non-credit factors or that are largely idiosyncratic.
criteria.rationale: The sleeve determines which preference set binds, what return bar applies, and what liquidity and equity-beta constraints the position must respect; an undefined macro or policy overlay inside a single-country fund can change all three.
criteria.finding: The materials say the strategy has a 'macro/policy coordination component' but never define it, and the asset class is recorded as unknown.
criteria.source: Key facts: 'Japan-focused investment strategy with macro/policy coordination component'; asset class listed as unknown
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the phrase 'macro/policy coordination component' is nowhere defined in the materials and could mean policy-linked or government capital, a state-coordinated co-investment programme, or a macro overlay on the portfolio, each of which would place the fund in a different sleeve; the investment-restrictions clause of the limited partnership agreement (LPA) and a direct question to the manager would settle it.

criteria.title: Equity-like return bar
criteria.preference: A Private Growth fund must plausibly clear equity-like return objectives; where the payoff is capped or credit-like, there must be a structural reason it still clears, such as government leverage, hybrid equity participation, a scarce-capital niche, or value on the buy.
criteria.rationale: Private Growth is the portfolio's growth engine, so a strategy that cannot clear equity-like returns belongs in another sleeve or nowhere; the test is applied before any qualitative view of the manager is formed.
criteria.finding: No target net internal rate of return (IRR), no target net multiple on invested capital (MOIC) and no gross-to-net assumption appears anywhere in the materials, and the asset class is not stated.
criteria.source: Key facts; target return not stated
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the materials state no target net IRR or net MOIC and do not name the asset class, leaving no basis on which to judge whether the fund clears the equity-like bar; the return targets in the private placement memorandum and the gross-to-net bridge would settle it.

criteria.title: Realisations, not marks
criteria.preference: Judge a manager on distributions to paid-in capital (DPI) and realised exits rather than on carrying values; a low DPI or largely unrealised record is a monitorable that is not set aside.
criteria.rationale: Unrealised marks are the manager's own valuations and can sustain an apparent record for years, whereas realised proceeds are the only evidence that the process converts into cash for limited partners (LPs).
criteria.finding: The fund is numbered 10, which implies a series of predecessor vintages, but the materials contain no DPI, total value to paid-in (TVPI), net IRR or realisation history for any prior fund.
criteria.source: Fund name 'Global Brain Flagship Fund 10'; no performance data in the materials
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the materials carry no performance figures whatsoever, which is a gap for a tenth fund where a realised record spanning multiple vintages should exist and be testable; fund-by-fund net DPI, TVPI and IRR by vintage, split realised versus unrealised, would settle it.

criteria.title: Practical drivers, bench and key-person cover
criteria.preference: Identify who actually drives sourcing, underwriting and value creation, test bench depth against fund size, and check that the legal key-person clause covers those real drivers rather than a nominal list.
criteria.rationale: Key-person clauses frequently protect the wrong people, and a bench that exists on slides rather than in practice is the common failure mode when a fund steps up in size; where the clause misses the true risk it becomes a negotiation target.
criteria.finding: The materials name one individual, Hiroshi Shimazu, Managing Partner, as the contact, and say nothing about investment team size, tenure, succession or the key-person clause.
criteria.source: Intro email contact line
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the only person named in the materials is the fundraising contact, Hiroshi Shimazu, Managing Partner, and a fundraising contact is not evidence of who drives investment decisions; the team section of the private placement memorandum, partner-level attribution of prior deals, and the key-person clause in the LPA would settle it.

criteria.title: Fund size and hard cap
criteria.preference: Establish the target fund size, negotiate a hard cap where one is absent, and treat a manager-imposed capacity limit as a different thing from a demand-driven close.
criteria.rationale: Fund size drives idea dilution: as assets grow, a manager adds opportunities to stay invested, spreading the team across more companies and lowering average idea quality, which makes the cap a return-protection term rather than an administrative one.
criteria.finding: No target size, hard cap or predecessor fund size is stated; the only size-adjacent statement is that the first close 'may serve as final close due to strong demand', which describes demand rather than a limit the manager has imposed on itself.
criteria.source: Key facts: first close 'may serve as final close due to strong demand'
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the materials give no target size or hard cap, and the 'strong demand' line is the manager's own account of its fundraise rather than evidence of capacity discipline; the target size, hard cap and predecessor fund sizes would settle it, and where no cap exists it becomes a side-letter item.

criteria.title: Position count, check size and partner bandwidth
criteria.preference: Set out the number of portfolio companies, check size and single-asset concentration, and convert concentration into basis points (bps) of total portfolio exposure against internal limits.
criteria.rationale: Bandwidth risk rises with more portfolio companies, more boards and more follow-ons rather than with concentration, unless the manager has a scaled bench and the systems to carry the load.
criteria.finding: The materials state no target number of portfolio companies, no check size, no ownership target and no follow-on reserve policy.
criteria.source: Key facts; portfolio construction not addressed
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the materials say nothing about how the fund will be constructed, so neither the concentration in bps nor the boards-per-partner load can be calculated; the target company count, average and maximum check size, reserve ratio and current boards per investment partner would settle it.

facts.label: Strategy
facts.value: Japan-focused flagship fund with a 'macro/policy coordination component'; asset class not stated

screen.not_covered: Economics, fund size, target return, track record, team depth and portfolio construction: the materials are a first-close invitation rather than an offering.
open_questions: What is the asset class and stage (venture, growth, buyout, or other), and does the payoff shape clear equity-like Private Growth return objectives?

What does the 'macro/policy coordination component' mean in practice: policy-linked or government capital, a state-coordinated co-investment programme, or a macro overlay on the portfolio? This is what makes the sleeve unclear.
What are the net DPI, TVPI and net IRR by vintage for the nine predecessor funds, split realised versus unrealised?
What is the target fund size, and is there a hard cap?
What are the management fee, carried interest, hurdle and GP commitment, and is a quantified first-close or relationship discount available?
Will a subsequent closing be available after the end-of-2026 first close, or is the window genuinely single?
Beyond Hiroshi Shimazu, who drives sourcing, underwriting and value creation; how large is the investment team relative to fund size; and whom does the key-person clause name?
What is the target number of portfolio companies, the average and maximum check size, the reserve policy, and the current boards per investment partner?
screen.summary: No view can be formed on these materials. They establish the fund name (Global Brain Flagship Fund 10, GB-X Japan Fund L.P.), a Japan geography, an end-of-2026 first close and one named contact, and nothing else. Three things drive the conclusion. First, the asset class is not stated, so the fund cannot even be assigned to Private Growth or Diversifiers, and the undefined 'macro/policy coordination component' is the specific phrase that makes that classification ambiguous rather than a formality. Second, with no target return, fund size, fee terms, track record or portfolio construction data, every substantive preference is unevidenced rather than met or failed, and for a tenth fund the absence of realised DPI and TVPI is the gap that most needs closing first. Third, the one deal-specific risk that is evidenced is the timetable: the first close 'may serve as final close due to strong demand', which is the manager's own framing and would compress the entire underwrite into a single window. The offer of virtual data room access is table stakes and is not itself a reason to proceed. Recommended next step is to open the VDR, confirm whether a subsequent closing exists, and pull the return targets, fee schedule and fund-by-fund realised performance before committing analyst time or capital.

criteria.title: Concentration tolerated only where the payoff shape justifies it
criteria.preference: Concentration tolerance depends on payoff shape: accepted in venture because power-law outcomes offset losses, disliked where per-asset upside is capped, and in private real assets managed through sizing plus explicit downside assumptions.
criteria.rationale: A concentrated book is only rational where one winner can pay for the losers; where each asset's upside is bounded, the same concentration simply raises the chance that a single execution failure sets the whole fund return.
criteria.finding: The programme is Japan hospitality and tourism built around one named development, Myoko, under the Six Senses and MGallery brands, with no other assets, no position count and no single-asset cap given. Ground-up development upside is bounded by yield on cost and exit pricing, while failure to deliver or stabilise leaves a partly built specialist asset in a regional ski market.
criteria.source: Opportunity summary, Key facts (geographic focus; investment strategy); Private Growth preferences 1.5
criteria.assessment: Not a fit because the evidenced structure puts the fund's return on one development location where per-asset upside is bounded by yield on cost and exit pricing, which is the payoff shape Weybourne's concentration tolerance is explicitly not calibrated for outside venture.

criteria.title: Concentration sized in basis points against internal limits
criteria.preference: Translate concentration risk into basis points (bps) of portfolio exposure and compare against internal single-asset limits, rather than leaving it as a qualitative statement.
criteria.rationale: Sizing is the control that makes a concentrated, execution-dependent asset survivable at portfolio level; a risk that is only described cannot be bounded.
criteria.finding: The materials give no target fund size, no hard cap, no expected number of assets, no development budget and no minimum commitment, so no exposure figure can be computed. A virtual data room (VDR) and in-person meetings are offered in place of figures.
criteria.source: Opportunity summary, Key facts (fund actively raising; VDR and in-person meetings offered)
criteria.assessment: A fit only if a commitment is sized in basis points at the level Weybourne reserves for concentrated, single-location real-asset exposure, which requires the fund size and asset count the materials do not yet give.

criteria.title: Cross-fund transactions at arm's length, with LPAC oversight
criteria.preference: Cross-fund deals and continuation vehicles are treated as alignment and loss-of-control risks; in platform builders they must be managed through arm's-length pricing, independent valuation and Limited Partner Advisory Committee (LPAC) oversight.
criteria.rationale: A manager running successive funds in the same theme can move assets, or their financing, between vehicles at prices it sets itself, transferring value between its own investor groups.
criteria.finding: Patience Capital Group (PCG) has at least two prior vehicles, Astro 1 and Astro 2, the latter considered by Weybourne, and the new fund targets the same country and sector. Whether the Tourism Fund acquires from, co-invests with, or takes over developments from the Astro funds is not stated, and no valuation or consent policy is described.
criteria.source: Opportunity summary, Key facts (previous PCG fund: Astro 2; Astro 1 performance)
criteria.assessment: A fit only if the Tourism Fund is barred from transacting with, or co-investing alongside, the Astro funds other than at independently valued arm's-length pricing with Limited Partner Advisory Committee (LPAC) consent.

criteria.title: Downside first: what has to happen for us to lose money
criteria.preference: Underwrite the downside before the base case, with an explicit scenario set and, in complex strategies, a severe-stress case that preserves capital.
criteria.rationale: Naming the loss path is what turns a return target into an underwriting; in development, the loss path is usually cost and time rather than demand.
criteria.finding: No downside case, construction contracting detail, contingency, opening date, occupancy or average daily rate (ADR) assumption, exit cap rate or currency policy appears in the materials. The most obvious loss path is specific to this deal and unaddressed: a delayed or over-budget build meeting softer inbound demand if the yen strengthens, with the same yen move also cutting the unhedged translation of returns for a non-yen investor, so the demand case and the currency exposure sit on the same side of the trade.
criteria.source: Opportionity summary, Key facts (hospitality/tourism property development, Myoko); no downside or hedging content in the materials
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the materials contain no scenario set, no construction or opening assumptions and no hedging policy, so the loss path cannot be assessed; a cost-overrun, delayed-opening and occupancy-shortfall case, the construction contracts, and the fund's currency policy would settle it.

criteria.title: A repeatable edge that answers "why them?"
criteria.preference: Back managers whose advantage is concrete and repeatable (proprietary information, pre-emptive or bilateral sourcing, in-house operating capability, execution at scale); if the edge is not structural, underwrite as commodity beta and demand commodity pricing, or pass.
criteria.rationale: Returns above the asset class come from an engine that keeps working across deals; without one, the manager is selling market exposure at active fees.
criteria.finding: The differentiators named are the Six Senses and MGallery brand affiliations, which any owner-developer can license, and the location itself. Nothing describes how the Myoko site was assembled, whether PCG had access ahead of competing bidders, or what in-house development and hotel asset-management capability it holds.
criteria.source: Opportunity summary, Key facts (investment strategy: Six Senses, MGallery)
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the materials present brands and a location rather than an origination, information or operating engine, and brand affiliation available to any owner cannot carry the "why them?" test; land assembly and site-control history, plus the in-house development and asset-management bench, would settle it.

criteria.title: Realisations, not marks
criteria.preference: Weigh distributions to paid-in capital (DPI) and realised outcomes; marks alone are insufficient, and early performance inside a J-curve must be interpreted with care.
criteria.rationale: In development strategies, a carried valuation reflects the manager's own assumptions about an asset that is not yet finished or trading, so an internal rate of return can be reported long before any cash comes back.
criteria.finding: The only performance figure is Astro 1 at approximately 17.5% against a 15% target. Whether that is gross or net, realised or based on unrealised valuations, who valued the assets, and over what period, is not stated. Astro 2's performance is not given, and no return target is stated for the Tourism Fund.
criteria.source: Opportunity summary, Key facts (Astro 1 Fund performance: ~17.5% vs 15% target)
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because approximately 17.5% against a 15% target, with no gross-versus-net basis, no distributions to paid-in capital (DPI) and no valuation source, does not establish whether the prior fund returned cash to investors.

criteria.title: Real bench and the practical key people, not only the legal clause
criteria.preference: Identify who actually drives origination, underwriting and value creation, test bench depth against fund size, look for deliberate succession, and check the key-person clause protects against the real risk.
criteria.rationale: A multi-year construction and hotel-stabilisation programme depends on named development and asset-management operators, and a clause drafted around figureheads leaves investors unprotected if those operators leave.
criteria.finding: The only individual named is Philippe Merette, Head of Equity Capital Markets, a capital-raising role. No development lead, hotel asset-management team, investment committee, headcount or key-person clause is described.
criteria.source: Opportunity summary, Key facts (contact: Philippe Merette, Head of Equity Capital Markets)
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the materials name a capital-markets contact and no investment, development or asset-management personnel, so the practical key people cannot be identified; an organisation chart, deal-level attribution for Astro 1, and the key-person clause would settle it.

criteria.title: Terms as a return and alignment lever, priced off the relationship
criteria.preference: Treat terms as both a net-return lever and an alignment tool: quantify first-close and size-break fee savings, seek relationship or platform economics, and use side letters and hard caps for governance and scale discipline.
criteria.rationale: Fees are the one part of the return that is known at signing, and a live raise plus an existing relationship is the only moment at which they are negotiable.
criteria.finding: No management fee, carry, preferred return, waterfall type, general partner commitment, hard cap or fund size appears in the materials, although the fund is actively raising and Weybourne has prior engagement with the manager through Astro 2.
criteria.source: Opportunity summary, Key facts (fund actively raising; previous PCG fund: Astro 2 considered by Weybourne)
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the materials state no economics at all, so the net-return effect of the terms is unknown, while the live raise and the prior Astro 2 engagement are the levers for a quantified first-close or relationship discount and a hard cap.

criteria.title: Blind pool justified against the existing roster
criteria.preference: A blind pool must be justified by differentiation from the existing manager roster, and there is an explicit "do we need this fund?" test even where the relationship is good.
criteria.rationale: Discretionary capital and identified-asset capital are different underwritings; the first is a bet on the manager's future selection, the second on a specific asset we can diligence now.
criteria.finding: It is not established whether the vehicle is a blind pool or a defined-asset vehicle: the fund is described as actively raising with one named development and two named hotel brands, but no asset schedule, pipeline, investment period or diversification limit is given. No comparison against existing Japan or hospitality exposure is offered.
criteria.source: Opportunity summary, Key facts (fund actively raising; Myoko development)
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the materials do not establish whether capital is committed to an identified asset set or to a discretionary pool, which is the first thing the "do we need this fund?" test turns on.

criteria.title: Sector and geography specialist rather than generalist
criteria.preference: Prefer specialists in a defined vertical or niche over generalists, on the basis that focused coverage with a structured framework compounds knowledge and access.
criteria.rationale: Repeat exposure to the same segment builds the target knowledge, local relationships and operating pattern recognition that a generalist has to buy in deal by deal.
criteria.finding: PCG is on at least its third vehicle in one country and one sector: Astro 1, Astro 2 and now the Japan Tourism Fund, all Japan hospitality and tourism, with the current fund centred on Myoko.
criteria.source: Opportunity summary, Key facts (fund; geographic focus; previous PCG fund)
criteria.assessment: A fit because the manager runs successive vehicles in a single country and single sector rather than a generalist mandate, which is the focused coverage Weybourne prefers, though the structured diligence framework that usually accompanies it is not evidenced here.

fit_points: A fit because the manager runs successive vehicles in a single country and single sector rather than a generalist mandate, which is the focused coverage Weybourne prefers, though the structured diligence framework that usually accompanies it is not evidenced here.
non_fit_points: Not a fit because the evidenced structure puts the fund's return on one development location where per-asset upside is bounded by yield on cost and exit pricing, which is the payoff shape Weybourne's concentration tolerance is explicitly not calibrated for outside venture.
open_questions: Is this a single-asset Myoko vehicle or a diversified Japan tourism programme: how many assets, what is the investment period, and is any capital already deployed?

What are the target fund size, hard cap, target net return, management fee, carry, preferred return and waterfall type, and is a first-close or relationship discount available given the prior Astro 2 engagement?
Is Astro 1's approximately 17.5% gross or net, and is it realised (distributions to paid-in capital, DPI) or based on unrealised valuations, valued by whom? What is Astro 2 marked at?
Will the Tourism Fund acquire assets from, co-invest with, or assume developments from Astro 1 or Astro 2, and on what pricing, independent valuation and consent basis?

Who leads site origination, development management and hotel asset management, as distinct from capital raising, what is the headcount against the build programme, and what does the key-person clause cover?

What is the development status: land control and permits, fixed-price versus cost-plus construction contracts, contingency, expected opening dates, and the economics of the Six Senses and MGallery management or licence agreements?
What is the currency exposure and hedging policy for a non-yen investor, and how is the inbound-demand case stress tested against a stronger yen?
What are the downside and severe-stress cases on cost overrun, delayed opening, occupancy and average daily rate (ADR) shortfall, and exit cap rate expansion, and what do they do to capital?
What is the assumed exit route for stabilised Japanese resort hotels, and what comparable transactions support it?
screen.summary: Screen as unclear, and do not progress on these materials: what has been provided is a teaser plus an invitation to a virtual data room (VDR), with fund size, terms, team, asset schedule and return target all unstated. Two things drive the view. First, despite the private equity label the engine is ground-up luxury hospitality development concentrated on one named location, Myoko, so upside is bounded by yield on cost and exit pricing while the downside runs to a partly built specialist asset in a regional ski market; that is the payoff shape Weybourne's concentration tolerance is least calibrated for, and it places the fund in the private real assets coverage area rather than buyout. Second, no repeatable edge is in evidence: the differentiators named are the Six Senses and MGallery affiliations, which any owner-developer can license, so on what is in hand this would be underwritten as commodity real-asset beta. The one supportive data point, Astro 1 at approximately 17.5% against a 15% target, is unusable until we know whether it is gross or net and whether it rests on realisations or on marks of an in-progress development. The most obvious deal-specific risk is not addressed anywhere in the materials: a delayed or over-budget build meeting softer inbound demand if the yen strengthens, with the same move cutting the unhedged yen translation of returns, so the demand case and the currency exposure sit on the same side of the trade. Next step is the VDR and a meeting focused on asset count, terms, the development contracts and Astro realisations.

criteria.title: Sleeve classification before anything else
criteria.preference: An opportunity must map to Private Growth, Public Growth or Diversifiers, with Diversifier status determined by whether returns are driven by non-equity/non-credit common factors or are largely idiosyncratic.
criteria.finding: The materials give a manager name (Horizon Capital AG) and the purpose of the contact (a personal coffee meeting). No fund, asset class, geography, structure or return driver is stated.

criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the materials name only the manager and the meeting request, with no fund, asset class, geography or return driver stated, so no sleeve can be assigned; a one-line description of the vehicle being raised, its asset class and its target geography would settle it.

criteria.title: Repeatable, structural edge rather than a claim
criteria.preference: The 'why them' must be concrete and repeatable - sourcing, information, operational or execution-at-scale edge - and quantifiable where claimed (countable relationships, meetings, coverage).

criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the materials contain no description of process, sourcing or claimed advantage of any kind; a deck or strategy summary setting out how the manager originates and wins deals would settle it.

criteria.preference: Fees are justified only by documented historical alpha; for Private Growth, a track record with realisations and DPI rather than marks alone.

criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because no return, vintage or realisation data has been provided at all; audited or GP-reported net returns by fund, with DPI, would settle it.

criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because no target return or payoff shape is stated, so the opportunity cannot be tested against either the equity-like Private Growth bar or the Diversifiers objectives; a target net return and target fund size would settle it.

criteria.title: Terms as a return and alignment lever
criteria.preference: Quantified fee savings from first close or size breaks, key-person tightening, hard caps and side-letter protections.

criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because no economic or governance terms have been disclosed; a term sheet or LPA summary covering fee, carry, hurdle, hard cap and key-person provisions would settle it.

criteria.title: Capacity discipline and hard caps
criteria.preference: Manager-imposed capacity limits, soft closes and hard caps are read as prioritising performance over asset gathering; scalability matters where the sleeve needs to stay meaningful.
criteria.finding: No fund size, hard cap or capacity position is disclosed.

criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because not a single individual, team size or tenure figure appears in the materials; a team page with named partners, tenure and attribution of prior deals would settle it.

criteria.preference: An explicit 'do we need this fund' test, including overlap with existing managers, redundancy with correlated strategies, and a cap of 15-18 active managers in Public Growth.

criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the strategy is not identified, so overlap and redundancy against the existing manager roster cannot be computed; naming the strategy and its top exposures would settle it.

criteria.title: Live answers versus prior materials
criteria.preference: Inconsistency or hedging between a manager's live answers and their deck or prior messaging is treated as a core diligence flag.
criteria.finding: There are no prior materials and no recorded meeting, so there is no baseline to test a live answer against.

criteria.title: Approach is a relationship contact, not an offer
criteria.preference: Findings must be tied to the opportunity's specifics; diligence items must be realistically obtainable.

screen.not_covered: Everything of substance: no fund, strategy, geography, team, track record, terms, size or structure is addressed anywhere in the materials.
open_questions: Which entity is 'Horizon Capital AG', and is a fund actually being raised, or is this purely a relationship introduction?
What strategy, asset class and geography would the vehicle pursue, and does it sit in Private Growth, Public Growth or Diversifiers?
What is the target size, hard cap and target net return, and what is the current fundraising status?
What is the firm's attributable track record by fund, including realised DPI rather than marks alone?
Who are the named individuals driving origination and value creation, and what is their prior attribution?
What are the headline economics: management fee, carry, hurdle, key-person provisions and any first-close discount?
Has anyone at Weybourne met this manager before, and does the strategy overlap with an existing manager?
screen.summary: There is nothing here to screen. The materials consist of a personal coffee meeting request from Horizon Capital AG, with no fund named, no asset class, no geography and no extracted facts, so every documented preference tested comes back unevidenced rather than pass or fail. The sleeve cannot be assigned, which means even the threshold question of which return bar applies (equity-like for Private Growth, or the drawdown, equity-beta and liquidity objectives for Diversifiers) is unanswerable. The deal-specific risk worth naming is that the approach is not tied to any identified vehicle: we do not know whether a raise exists, and walking into the meeting without that is the difference between a relationship coffee and a screen. Take the meeting on relationship terms if the time is cheap, but ask for a one-page strategy summary, target size and prior fund performance beforehand so the conversation starts from something testable.

criteria.title: Materials sufficient to screen at all
criteria.preference: Do not accept the manager's own framing at face value; evaluate the underlying engine, and only list diligence items that are realistically obtainable.
criteria.finding: The entire record is an intermediary introduction email from Pangaea Alts naming Stakeboat Capital Fund III (mid-market private equity (PE), $250m target, India, healthcare / business-to-business (B2B) technology / manufacturing) alongside an unrelated second fund, plus meeting availability 24 Sept - 2 Oct in Singapore. There is no deck, no private placement memorandum, no track record page and no independent web research in the file.
criteria.source: Intro email from Pangaea Alts (key facts list)
criteria.assessment: A fit only if the manager or intermediary provides a deck, prior-fund performance and terms ahead of the Singapore window, since at present there is no underlying engine to evaluate and no manager framing to test.

criteria.title: Terms as a return and alignment lever, with first-close discounts quantified
criteria.preference: Quantify fee savings from first close and size breaks, and use side letters for key-person tightening, reputational carve-outs, tax protections and hard caps.
criteria.finding: No management fee, carry, hurdle, general partner (GP) commitment, hard cap or close schedule is stated. The only timing signal is that the fund is being actively marketed into SuperReturn 2026, which implies a fundraise still open.
criteria.source: Intro email; key facts (target size $250m, Fund III vintage, meeting 24 Sept - 2 Oct)
criteria.assessment: A fit only if an early-close or relationship discount is available and quantified against the standard fee load, and if India-specific tax and repatriation protections can be secured by side letter, none of which the materials address.

criteria.title: Repeatable, structural edge ("why them?")
criteria.preference: Prioritise managers whose edge is concrete and repeatable: proprietary information, bilateral or systematic sourcing, in-house operating capability, or execution at scale.
criteria.finding: The materials describe only the sector scope (healthcare, B2B technology, manufacturing) and the geography. Nothing is said about how deals are originated, whether the firm has an operating bench, or what it does that competing India mid-market managers do not.
criteria.source: Intro email; key facts (mid-market PE, healthcare / B2B tech / manufacturing)
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the materials name a sector focus and nothing about the origination or value-creation engine; a deal-by-deal sourcing history for Funds I and II, showing which were bilateral versus intermediated, would settle it.

criteria.title: Equity-like return objective, net of the India-specific drag
criteria.preference: Private Growth is a portfolio growth engine with default expectations of equity-like returns; a strategy must plausibly clear that bar.
criteria.finding: No target gross or net return, no target multiple on invested capital (MOIC) or internal rate of return (IRR), and no statement of the currency in which returns are underwritten or whether any hedging is contemplated.
criteria.source: Intro email; key facts (no return target stated)
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the materials state no return target at all, so the bar cannot be tested; the fund's target net United States dollar (USD) IRR and its assumed Indian rupee (INR) depreciation would settle it.

criteria.title: Realised distributions, not marks
criteria.preference: Distributions to paid-in (DPI) and realisations matter; marks alone are insufficient, and low DPI or an unrealised record is a live monitorable.
criteria.finding: The fund is described as "Fund III vintage". No performance, DPI, total value to paid-in (TVPI) or exit history for Funds I or II is given, and the vintage years of the prior funds are not stated.
criteria.source: Intro email; key facts (Fund III vintage)
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because a third fund implies a prior record that the materials simply do not present; audited Fund I and Fund II performance with a realisation-by-realisation exit list, including holding periods and exit routes, would settle it.

criteria.title: Control, and loss of control in minority positions
criteria.preference: Strong preference for control; minority positions and the resulting loss of control over exit timing are treated as a material downside channel.
criteria.finding: The fund is labelled "mid-market PE" with no statement of whether it takes majority control, structured minority stakes or growth-equity minorities, and no statement of board rights, drag rights or exit consents.
criteria.source: Intro email; key facts (mid-market PE)
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the materials do not say whether Stakeboat buys control or minority positions, a distinction that changes the underwrite entirely; the split of Fund II deals by control versus minority, with governance rights per deal, would settle it.

criteria.title: Portfolio construction and single-asset concentration in basis points
criteria.preference: Prefer explicit portfolio-construction constraints, and translate concentration into basis points (bps) of portfolio exposure rather than qualitative statements.
criteria.finding: Only the $250m target size is given. Target number of positions, maximum single-asset cap, expected average cheque size and any sector or sub-sector limits are absent.
criteria.source: Intro email; key facts (target size $250m)
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because fund size alone does not imply a position count, so no bps exposure can be computed; the target number of portfolio companies and the single-asset cap in the limited partnership agreement would settle it.

criteria.title: Practical key people and succession, tested against the legal clause
criteria.preference: Identify who truly drives sourcing, underwriting and value creation, test bench depth against fund size, and check the key-person clause protects against the real risk.
criteria.finding: No principals are named, no team size is given, no carry distribution is described, and the key-person clause is not referenced.
criteria.source: Intro email (no team detail)
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the materials name no individual at the firm, let alone the driver of origination; a team page with tenure, attribution of Fund I and II deals by partner, and the draft key-person language would settle it.

criteria.title: Exit liquidity in a single-country emerging market
criteria.preference: In single-country emerging-market exposure, exit liquidity and strategic-sector constraints are treated as central considerations rather than assumed away.
criteria.finding: The materials state only that the fund is India-focused. Nothing is said about exit routes (initial public offering on Indian exchanges, strategic sale, sponsor-to-sponsor), the historic exit mix of prior funds, or repatriation and withholding treatment.
criteria.source: Intro email; key facts (India-focused)
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because geography is stated and exit mechanics are not; the realised exit route and time-to-exit for every Fund I and Fund II disposal, plus the fund's tax domicile and repatriation structure, would settle it.

facts.label: Strategy
facts.value: India mid-market private equity (healthcare, business-to-business (B2B) technology, manufacturing)

screen.not_covered: Everything beyond strategy label, geography, fund number and target size: no track record, team, terms, portfolio construction, control posture, exit history or tax structure.
open_questions: What are audited Fund I and Fund II net returns, DPI and TVPI by vintage, and what did each realised exit actually return?
Does Stakeboat take control positions or minority stakes, and what governance and exit rights attach to each?
Who originates and underwrites, how many investment professionals are there, and does the key-person clause name the actual drivers?
What is the target net USD IRR and MOIC, and what INR depreciation assumption sits behind it?
How were prior-fund exits achieved (Indian public listing, strategic, sponsor-to-sponsor), and over what holding periods?
What are the fee, carry, hurdle and GP commitment, and is a first-close or relationship discount available given the fundraise is live into SuperReturn 2026?
How is the fund structured for Indian tax and repatriation, and what withholding drag reaches a Weybourne-level investor?
What is the target number of portfolio companies and the single-asset cap, so concentration can be expressed in bps of portfolio?
Is Omnivore Venture Fund III ($225m early-stage impact VC) wanted as a separate screen, or declined at the intermediary stage?
screen.summary: This cannot be screened on what we hold. The file is a single intermediary introduction from Pangaea Alts giving four data points: India mid-market private equity (PE) across healthcare, business-to-business (B2B) technology and manufacturing; a $250m target; Fund III; and meeting availability 24 Sept - 2 Oct in Singapore. There is no deck, no prior-fund performance, no team detail, no terms and no independent research, so every preference that bears on the decision is unevidenced rather than passed or failed. Two points are worth making before any meeting is booked. First, the deal-specific risk that dominates and maps to no single preference line is that a single-country India fund must clear an equity-like USD return bar after rupee depreciation and Indian exit friction, and the materials state neither a return target nor a single realised exit from the two prior funds: a third fund with an undisclosed record is the thing to press on. Second, the most decision-changing unknown is whether Stakeboat buys control or takes minority growth stakes, since that determines whether exit timing sits with us or with a founder. The practical next step is to request the deck, audited Fund I and II performance with an exit-by-exit realisation schedule, and the term sheet, then decide whether the Singapore slot is worth taking. Omnivore Venture Fund III ($225m early-stage impact venture capital) arrived in the same email and is a separate strategy requiring its own screen.

criteria.title: Sleeve classification before anything else
criteria.preference: An opportunity must be mapped to a sleeve (Private Growth, Public Growth or Diversifiers), and a Diversifier only qualifies where returns are driven by non-equity/non-credit common factors or are largely idiosyncratic.
criteria.finding: The materials state only that an internal recommendation on Trivest has been prepared and circulated for feedback. Asset class, geography and strategy are all absent.
criteria.source: Intro email ("Investment Recommendation document prepared"; "Limited details provided in email itself")
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the email names the opportunity and nothing else, so the fund cannot be mapped to a coverage area, let alone tested against the Diversifiers classification lens; the recommendation document would settle it in one line.

criteria.title: Equity-like return bar for Private Growth
criteria.preference: A Private Growth fund must plausibly clear equity-like return objectives, and where the payoff is credit-like or capped it must have a structural reason (government leverage, hybrid equity participation, niche capital gap, value on the buy) that still gets it there.
criteria.finding: No target net return, gross return, payoff shape or structural feature is stated anywhere in the materials.
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the materials give no return target and no description of the payoff shape, so there is nothing to test the Private Growth return bar against; the target net MOIC and net IRR in the recommendation document would settle it.

criteria.title: Repeatable edge, not a table-stakes claim
criteria.preference: The "why them" must be a concrete and repeatable sourcing, information, operational or execution-at-scale advantage; absent that, underwrite as commodity beta and demand commodity pricing or pass.
criteria.finding: No strategy description, sourcing model, operating capability or claimed differentiator appears in the materials.
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the materials contain no description of how the manager sources or creates value, so there is no engine to evaluate behind the framing; the Strategy and Why attractive sections of the recommendation document would settle it.

criteria.title: Downside-first underwriting
criteria.preference: Underwrite what has to happen to lose money, with explicit scenario sets where the strategy is special situations or complex credit, and concentration translated into basis points of portfolio exposure.
criteria.finding: No scenario analysis, downside case, loss driver or sizing figure is present in the materials.
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the materials carry no downside case or proposed commitment size, so the concentration cannot be converted into basis points against internal limits; the Sizing section and any stress case in the recommendation document would settle it.

criteria.title: Real bench, deliberate succession, and a key-person clause that bites
criteria.preference: Test whether the bench is scaled to fund size, whether succession is named and deliberate, and whether the legal key-person clause covers the people who actually drive origination, underwriting and value creation.
criteria.finding: No named principals, team size, tenure or key-person terms appear in the materials.
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because no individual at the manager is named in the materials, so neither practical key-person dependence nor the adequacy of the legal clause can be assessed; the Team section and the LPA key-person provision would settle it.

criteria.title: Terms as a return and alignment lever
criteria.preference: Quantify fee savings from first close or size breaks, evaluate the fee-structure choice as an underwriting lever, check the GP commit trend, and negotiate hard caps and side-letter protections where absent.
criteria.finding: No management fee, carry, hurdle, GP commitment, fund size or hard cap is stated.
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the materials disclose no economics at all, so no fee saving can be quantified and no negotiation lever identified; the Key terms section of the recommendation document would settle it.

criteria.title: Control, cross-fund deals and continuation vehicles
criteria.preference: Cross-fund deals, minority rollovers and continuation vehicles are treated as material loss-of-control and alignment risks; in secondaries, minority status is acceptable only where a fully aligned bloc holds verified majority control.
criteria.finding: The materials do not say whether this is a primary commitment, a secondary, a continuation vehicle or a co-investment.
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the transaction type is not stated, so it is not even known whether the control framework applies; identifying whether this is a blind-pool primary or a single-asset secondary would settle it.

criteria.title: Track record with realisations, not marks
criteria.preference: Distributions to paid-in capital (DPI) and realisations carry weight; marks and unrealised performance alone are insufficient, and low DPI is a monitorable rather than something to overlook.
criteria.finding: No prior fund performance, vintage, DPI, total value to paid-in capital (TVPI) or realisation history is provided.
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because no performance data of any kind accompanies the email, so realised versus unrealised value cannot be separated; a net performance table by vintage would settle it.

criteria.title: Live answers tested against marketing materials
criteria.preference: Flag any inconsistency or hedging between what a manager said in a meeting, what the deck claims, and the answer given when questioned directly, as a core diligence concern.
criteria.finding: No meeting note, deck or manager statement is in the materials, so there is nothing to cross-check.
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because neither a meeting record nor the manager's own marketing materials were supplied, so the two cannot be set against each other; the meeting notes plus the deck would settle it.

criteria.title: Do we need this fund, and does it overlap what we already hold
criteria.preference: Apply an explicit "do we need this fund" test, and analyse overlap with existing platforms at look-through level, translated into basis points, particularly where the relationship is already strong.
criteria.finding: The materials do not indicate whether Weybourne has an existing relationship with this manager, holds prior vintages, or has look-through overlap with current holdings.
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the email establishes no relationship history or portfolio context, so neither the need test nor an overlap analysis can be run; our internal holdings record for this manager would settle it.

screen.not_covered: Everything of substance: the materials contain no strategy, geography, asset class, fund size, economics, team, track record or transaction type.
open_questions: Can the Investment Recommendation document itself be circulated, since the email refers to it but it is not attached?

The materials consist of an internal email stating that an Investment Recommendation on Trivest has been prepared and shared for feedback, with the document itself not attached and no strategy, asset class, geography, fund size, economics, team or track record given. Every preference tested therefore resolves to unevidenced, and the sleeve cannot be assigned. The most obvious deal-specific risk sits in the process rather than the fund: a document already titled \"Investment Recommendation\" is circulating for feedback before the team has seen the facts that would support or contradict it, which anchors the discussion on a conclusion nobody can yet check. The name Trivest is not, on its own, evidence of anything about the strategy, and no assumption has been made about it here. Send the recommendation document and the manager's materials, and this can be screened properly against the Private Growth framework.

criteria.title: Countable information edge for a geographic specialist
criteria.preference: Specialist managers must demonstrate a verifiable, quantifiable information advantage (offices in named cities, counted management meetings, counted expert relationships), not generic claims of expertise.
criteria.finding: The only edge described is a "concentrated long/short approach with stock selection focus". No office locations, team location, meeting counts, corporate-access statistics or other countable metric is given.
criteria.source: Intro email key facts (Ensor Partners introduction of Nimit, dT! Partners)
criteria.assessment: Not a fit because the edge as presented is "stock selection focus", which is a description of what every discretionary equity manager does and carries no countable metric of the kind P9.1 and P1.3 require.

criteria.title: Underperformance attributed to flows rather than process
criteria.preference: Judge the underlying return engine rather than the manager's framing, and treat a softer or self-serving explanation as a diligence flag rather than a fact.
criteria.finding: FY26 underperformance is attributed to Foreign Institutional Investor (FII) outflows and explicitly not to deterioration of the investment thesis; the follow-on point is a "strong recovery in FY27". No attribution data, gross/net exposure history or long-versus-short contribution is provided.
criteria.source: Intro email key facts
criteria.assessment: Not a fit because a long/short (L/S) manager whose losses are explained by market-wide foreign flows is describing beta and factor exposure it did not hedge, and the explanation is offered as an assertion with no long-book versus short-book attribution behind it.

criteria.title: Asia manager count and manager consolidation
criteria.preference: Asia can support at most two managers, and only where approaches are materially different; overall, prefer deepening existing manager relationships to adding a marginal new one, within a 15-18 active manager ceiling.
criteria.finding: This is a single-country India mandate. The approved Public Growth set already carries a thematic Asia manager with South East Asia weighting and a broad Emerging Market (EM) mandate covering India-region research (a 40-person team spanning Hong Kong, Mumbai and Sao Paulo).
criteria.source: Intro email (India-focused); Public Growth preferences P7.4, P7.1, P1.8, P4.1 evidence lines
criteria.assessment: A fit only if it displaces one of the two existing Asia mandates rather than becoming a third, and if the overlap of its India book against the incumbent broad Emerging Market (EM) manager's India exposure is measured and shown to be low.

criteria.title: Realised alpha as the fee hurdle
criteria.preference: Allocation rests on documented alpha that clears the fee level; alpha is the lead question and fees are only the hurdle it must clear.
criteria.finding: No return series, no benchmark, no alpha figure and no fee schedule appear in the materials. FY26 and FY27 are referenced only in direction ("underperformance", "strong recovery"), with no numbers.
criteria.source: Intro email key facts
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the materials contain no return, benchmark or fee figures at all; a monthly net return series since inception against the MSCI India index (or a stated benchmark), plus the management and performance fee terms, would settle it.

criteria.title: Track record length and through-cycle evidence
criteria.preference: 10-20+ years preferred; five years minimum for consideration, with offsetting factors such as prior track record elsewhere, and crisis behaviour assessed where a crisis fell inside the record.
criteria.finding: The materials reference only two fiscal years, FY26 and FY27. No inception date, no prior-firm history for Nimit, and no team background is given.
criteria.source: Intro email key facts
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the materials give no inception date or prior-firm record; the fund's launch date, an attributable track record for the portfolio manager before dT! Partners, and drawdown/recovery figures for the 2020 and 2022 episodes if they fall inside the record would settle it.

criteria.title: Concentration matched to monitoring and to liquidity terms
criteria.preference: Concentrated portfolios require evidence of monitoring depth, and redemption terms must match the diversification and liquidity of the book.
criteria.finding: The strategy is described as concentrated, but no position count, top-ten weight, single-name cap, market-cap distribution or redemption terms are stated.
criteria.source: Intro email key facts
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the materials name concentration without quantifying it or stating redemption terms; the position count, top-five and top-ten weights, the market-cap breakdown of the long book, and the dealing frequency, notice period and any lock or gate would settle it.

criteria.title: Return target for Emerging Market equity long/short
criteria.preference: Emerging Market (EM) equity long/short is expected to target 18-22% absolute net with 8-10% alpha over the relevant EM index, at 18-22% volatility.
criteria.finding: No target return, target alpha, volatility target or net exposure range is stated.
criteria.source: Intro email key facts
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the materials state no return or risk target; the fund's stated net return target, alpha target against its chosen India benchmark, realised volatility and net exposure range would settle it.

criteria.title: Local presence and language capability
criteria.preference: Managers in a single non-English-speaking market must have investment staff physically located there with native language capability.
criteria.finding: The manager is described only as "India-focused". Nothing in the materials states where the investment team sits or what languages it operates in.
criteria.source: Intro email (manager description)
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the materials do not say where the team is based; the office locations, headcount by location and language capability of the investment staff would settle it.

criteria.title: Operational rating and service providers
criteria.preference: Institutional administrator, Big 4 or equivalent auditor and independent prime brokerage, with the Operational Due Diligence (ODD) rating setting the maximum position size.
criteria.finding: No administrator, auditor, prime broker, domicile, Assets Under Management (AUM) figure or ODD rating is named anywhere in the materials.
criteria.source: Intro email key facts
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because the materials name no service providers or operational rating; the fund domicile, administrator, auditor, prime broker(s), current AUM and any existing Albourne ODD rating would settle it and would set the sizing ceiling before strategy merit is even reached.

criteria.title: Capacity discipline
criteria.preference: Manager-imposed capacity limits and soft-closes are read as prioritising performance over asset gathering.
criteria.finding: The approach came through a third-party business development introduction (Ensor Partners) for a meeting to discuss strategy and recent performance. No capacity statement, hard cap or soft-close is mentioned.
criteria.source: Intro email (Ensor Partners introducing Nimit for a business development meeting)
criteria.assessment: Unevidenced because an actively-marketed introduction says nothing either way about capacity policy; the stated strategy capacity in dollars, current AUM against it, and whether any capacity limit has ever been enforced would settle it.

Not a fit because a long/short (L/S) manager whose losses are explained by market-wide foreign flows is describing beta and factor exposure it did not hedge, and the explanation is offered as an assertion with no long-book versus short-book attribution behind it.

If Foreign Institutional Investor (FII) outflows drove FY26 underperformance, what were gross and net exposure through that period, and what was the short book doing?

screen.summary: Take the business development meeting, but treat this as a first conversation and not a screen that can be concluded. The materials are an introduction email with five bullet points: no returns, no fees, no terms, no team, no service providers, no Assets Under Management (AUM). Almost every binding Public Growth test therefore comes back unevidenced rather than passed or failed. Two things do stand out from what is there. First, the edge as described is \"concentrated long/short with stock selection focus\", which is the default description of a discretionary equity manager and carries none of the countable specialist metrics the framework requires of a single-country mandate. Second, FY26 underperformance is attributed to Foreign Institutional Investor (FII) outflows rather than the thesis, and a long/short manager explaining losses by market-wide foreign flows is describing unhedged beta and factor exposure; that attribution needs to be tested against long-book and short-book contribution data before it is accepted. Separately, a single-country India fund would be a third Asia mandate against a documented ceiling of two, so it has to earn its place by displacing an incumbent rather than sitting alongside them, and its India overlap with the existing broad Emerging Market (EM) manager needs measuring. The \"India valuation premium at a 20-year low\" point is an index-level entry argument and does not bear on whether this manager generates alpha.
